evidence: src/domain/errors.ts: DomainError, whose codes include 'insufficient_stock' and 'invalid_transition', is the only error type the domain uses.
src/domain/order.ts: ORDER_STATES is the single definition of the lifecycle; isOrderStatus and nextState both derive from it and throw DomainError('invalid_transition').

src/domain/order.ts: assertCancellable lists 'placed'/'paid'/'packed' as literals rather than deriving them from ORDER_STATES. This is a small redundancy inside one file, not a rule duplicated across files.
src/domain/product.ts: availableOf is the single definition of available stock and is reused by reserve and toStockLevel; reserve throws DomainError('insufficient_stock').
src/domain/product.ts: reserve/release/dispatch all work on the Product.reserved/onHand fields together as one cohesive stock-reservation concern.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The src/domain module holds one concern: the core order-fulfilment domain. It has an order lifecycle (order.ts), product stock reservation (product.ts) and a shared error type (errors.ts). Both entity files signal rule violations through the shared DomainError instead of using ad-hoc errors. Each invariant has a single home. The lifecycle sequence is defined once in ORDER_STATES, and isOrderStatus and nextState both derive from it. The stock-availability calculation is defined once in availableOf, and reserve and toStockLevel both reuse it. No file goes around the module's own abstractions. One small point: assertCancellable lists 'placed' | 'paid' | 'packed' literally instead of deriving them from ORDER_STATES. That logic sits in the same file, right next to the state list, and is not repeated anywhere else, so it is not a cross-file duplication that breaks cohesion. Also, release and dispatch do not guard against quantities going negative. That is about how correct the invariant is, not about the module's boundary or coherence.
